story: FERC opens a public comment window on the Alaska Energy Authority's proposal to divert Dixon Glacier meltwater into Bradley Lake, a scale check on what it costs Alaska to add power

claims.claim: The Alaska Energy Authority's non-capacity amendment application for the Bradley Lake Hydroelectric Project is docketed at FERC as Project No. 8221-124 and was filed on June 30, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Date Filed: June 30, 2026.
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, via govinfo.gov
claims.notes: FR Doc No. 2026-15691. AEA's own press release announcing the filing is dated 2026-07-20, three weeks after FERC's Date Filed. Use FERC's date.

claims.claim: FERC published the notice soliciting comments, motions to intervene and protests in the Federal Register on August 3, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Alaska Energy Authority; Notice of Application for Non-Capacity Amendment of License Accepted for Filing, Soliciting Comments, Motions To Intervene, and Protests
claims.notes: API returns publication_date 2026-08-03, agency FERC. The API record carries no comments_close_on field, so the deadline is cited to the notice body at C03.

claims.claim: Comments, motions to intervene and protests on the Dixon Diversion amendment are due by August 28, 2026 at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
claims.verbatim: Deadline for filing comments, motions to intervene, and protests: August 28, 2026 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, via govinfo.gov
claims.notes: The deck's call to action. 5:00 p.m. Eastern is 1:00 p.m. Alaska Daylight Time on August 28. Do not print an Alaska time without saying it is converted.

claims.claim: The amendment proposes a new diversion dam to divert meltwater and surface runoff coming from the Dixon Glacier into Bradley Lake.
claims.verbatim: a new diversion dam to divert meltwater and surface runoff coming from the Dixon Glacier
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, via govinfo.gov
claims.notes: Meltwater AND surface runoff, not just meltwater. Copy must not shorten to melting a glacier or imply the glacier is consumed.

claims.claim: The amendment would raise Bradley Lake's normal maximum operating pool elevation by approximately 16 feet through spillway modifications and raising the dam embankment.
claims.verbatim: Raising the normal maximum operating pool elevation of Bradley Lake by approximately 16 feet
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, via govinfo.gov
claims.notes: Corroborated independently by Petroleum News. Two sources agree on 16.

claims.claim: The amendment would install a 0.3 megawatt micro-hydro turbine in one of the Bradley Lake Dam's fishwater release valves.
claims.verbatim: a 0.3-megawatt (MW) micro-hydro turbine in one of the Bradley Lake Dam's fishwater release valves
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, via govinfo.gov
claims.notes: This turbine is the entire installed-capacity gain. It is a byproduct of the fishwater release, not the point of the project. The point is water volume, which raises energy without raising nameplate.

claims.claim: The project's installed capacity would rise from 119.7 megawatts to 120.0 megawatts, a gain of 0.3 megawatts.
claims.verbatim: increase the Bradley Lake Project's installed capacity from 119.7 MW to 120.0 MW
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, via govinfo.gov
claims.notes: AEA's own page rounds the existing plant to 120 MW. Cite FERC's 119.7 for the before figure. The 0.3 MW delta is the spine of the deck's scale check and must never appear without C08.

claims.claim: FERC's notice states the amendment would increase the project's average annual power generation by approximately 38 percent.
claims.verbatim: average annual power generation by approximately 38 percent.
claims.source_outlet: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, via govinfo.gov
claims.notes: A 38 percent gain in ENERGY against a 0.25 percent gain in CAPACITY. Never write 38 percent more capacity or 38 percent bigger. Applicant projection, so hedge as the application states.

claims.claim: The Alaska Energy Authority estimates the Dixon Diversion construction cost at approximately $400 million.
claims.verbatim: The estimated construction cost of the project is approximately $400 million.
claims.notes: Sponsor's own estimate and a construction cost, not a total project cost. AEA's separate Bradley Lake page lists the ORIGINAL 1991 project budget as $400 Million. Two unrelated $400 million figures exist thirty five years apart. Never place them side by side without distinguishing them. Page undated, date_of_source is the fetch date.

claims.claim: The Alaska Energy Authority's schedule for the Dixon Diversion is an estimated three years of study and permitting followed by three years of construction.
claims.verbatim: Estimated three years of study and permitting followed by three years of construction.
claims.notes: Sponsor projection. Say AEA estimates about six years rather than stating it as fact. The clock has not started; the amendment is still in comment.

claims.claim: The Dixon Diversion would be located five miles southwest of Bradley Lake and approximately 27 miles northeast of Homer on the Kenai Peninsula.
claims.verbatim: five miles southwest of Bradley Lake, approximately 27 miles northeast of Homer on the Kenai Peninsula
claims.notes: Geodata for the map slide. Homer is the recognisable anchor for a general audience.

claims.claim: From 1995 through 2020 the Bradley Lake Hydroelectric Project averaged 392,000 megawatt hours of generation annually.
claims.verbatim: From 1995 through 2020, the Project averaged 392,000 megawatt-hours annually
claims.notes: A 26-year historical average, not a current-year figure, and it must be labelled that way. Single-sourced to AEA, who own the project. Do not attribute to EIA; the EIA data browser could not be read.

claims.claim: Bradley Lake provides approximately 10 percent of the total annual power used by Railbelt utilities.
claims.verbatim: provides approximately 10 percent of the total annual power used by Railbelt utilities
claims.notes: Independently corroborated by Petroleum News on 2026-08-02. Two sources, one primary. Prefer AEA's wording, power used, over the trade paper's electricity demand.

claims.claim: The Bradley Lake project began operating in 1991 and delivers power at a cost of about four cents per kilowatt hour.
claims.verbatim: at a cost of about $0.04 per kilowatt-hour
claims.notes: The four cent figure is undated on an undated page and is likely legacy. Hedge as AEA puts the cost at about four cents, or omit.

claims.claim: Petroleum News reports the Dixon Diversion would move water to Bradley Lake through a 4.6 mile connecting tunnel.
claims.verbatim: 4.6-mile connecting tunnel
claims.notes: ATTRIBUTION CORRECTED. Not on either AEA page and not in the FERC notice. Survives only as a Petroleum News figure, byline Alan Bailey. Any slide using it must say reported by Petroleum News, never AEA says.

claims.claim: Petroleum News reports the expansion would produce enough additional renewable energy to power up to 30,000 homes.
claims.verbatim: enough additional renewable energy to power up to 30,000 homes
claims.notes: Up to is already a hedge in the source and the homes conversion is never defined. Internally consistent against C12 and C08 at roughly 5,000 kWh per home per year. Print as Petroleum News reports.

claims.claim: Petroleum News reports the expansion would displace around 1.5 billion cubic feet of natural gas per year for power generation.
claims.verbatim: around 1.5 billion cubic feet of natural gas per year for power generation
claims.notes: Projection, single-sourced to a trade outlet. Implies roughly 10,000 cubic feet per MWh, a reasonable Cook Inlet heat rate. Internally consistent. Hedge as Petroleum News reports.

claims.claim: Petroleum News reports that five Railbelt electric utilities receive Bradley Lake power across the transmission system.
claims.verbatim: Five Railbelt electricity utilities
claims.notes: Weakest of the Petroleum News set and uncorroborated on AEA's page. Usable as flavour, not as a headline number. If a slide needs reach, prefer AEA's about 75 percent of Alaska's population.

claims.claim: The Alaska Energy Authority board of directors endorsed a financing package for constructing the Bradley Lake Expansion Project on July 23, 2026.
claims.verbatim: The Alaska Energy Authority (AEA) Board of Directors has endorsed a financing package for constructing the Bradley Lake Expansion Project
claims.notes: Verified from the newsroom index. The individual release was not opened, so no dollar figure or financing structure is verified. Do not state how the project is being paid for.

claims.claim: The Department of the Air Force is offering approximately 4,700 acres of underutilized land across Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station for potential AI data center development.
claims.verbatim: The DAF is offering approximately 4,700 acres of underutilized land across Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base, and Clear Space Force Station.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Department of the Air Force
claims.notes: The deck's comparison anchor, and it is LAND, not POWER. A slide comparing 4,700 acres to 0.3 MW compares unlike units and must be written as two separate facts about ambition, never as a ratio.

claims.claim: The Air Force has identified twelve parcels at the three Alaska installations for potential AI data center development.
claims.verbatim: Twelve parcels have been identified for potential development.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Department of the Air Force
claims.notes: Identified for potential development. No parcel has been leased or awarded. Copy must keep the conditional.

claims.claim: Robert Moriarty, Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Installations, said the Alaska land offer supports the growing demands of the AI industry while generating value that directly supports Air Force missions.
claims.verbatim: By making this land available, we are supporting the growing demands of the AI industry while generating value that directly supports our missions and the readiness of our Airmen and Guardians.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Department of the Air Force
claims.notes: Verbatim quote confirmed on the fetched page. Safe to print in quotation marks with name and title.

claims.claim: Air Force solicitation AFCEC-26-R-0006 for AI data center development at the three Alaska installations was posted April 10, 2026, closed to proposals June 29, 2026, and was archived July 14, 2026 with no award posted.
claims.verbatim: Response/Close Date: June 29, 2026, 5:00 p.m. EDT
claims.notes: A mirror, not the primary record; SAM.gov returned an empty shell. Status shows Past Due, NOT Awarded, so write no award has been posted rather than no award was made. HigherGov's listed value range is machine-generated and labelled an AI estimate, so it must never be printed.

claims.claim: Alaska Public Media reported that Enstar has already had to turn away new large scale customers to focus on supplying existing ratepayers.
claims.verbatim: There is little interest from energy companies to expand production in Cook Inlet, and Enstar has already had to turn away new, large-scale customers to focus on supplying existing ratepayers, Sims said.
claims.notes: THIS IS THE REPORTER'S PARAPHRASE, NOT A DIRECT QUOTE. It may be attributed to Alaska Public Media reporting what Sims said. It may NEVER be set in quotation marks as Sims's words.

claims.claim: Enstar president John Sims said that if Southcentral Alaska has a winter like last year, the region is going to have significant challenges and will likely see rolling blackouts.
claims.verbatim: If we have a winter like we did last year, we are going to have significant challenges and likely see rolling blackouts.
claims.notes: A genuine verbatim direct quote, safe in quotation marks, attributed to John Sims, president of Enstar, via Alaska Public Media. The conditional must be preserved. Never print that Alaska will have rolling blackouts.

claims.claim: Applying the application's approximately 38 percent projected increase to Bradley Lake's 392,000 megawatt hour historical annual average implies roughly 149,000 additional megawatt hours a year, a figure calculated by Alaska.Ai rather than published by any party.
claims.verbatim: From 1995 through 2020, the Project averaged 392,000 megawatt-hours annually
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Energy Authority, arithmetic by Alaska.Ai
claims.notes: DERIVED, NOT SOURCED. No document states an absolute post-project figure. Must be visibly labelled as our calculation wherever it appears, including in the caption, and written with roughly. The 38 percent may be computed against a different baseline, which would move this number.

dropped: Enhanced Use Lease term of up to 50 years. The af.mil release states no term and HigherGov says the period is negotiated after selection. Not provable, not inferred.

The Air Force 100 MW per-project minimum. THE DECK'S ORIGINAL COMPARISON ANCHOR. Zero instances of 100 MW, megawatt or minimum in the af.mil release or the HigherGov description. Both scouts traced it to a single partisan outlet. MUST NOT BE PRINTED.
The Air Force $500 million per-project minimum. Same failure mode, same single advocacy source.

The Stak Energy North Slope campus at 1 to 3 gigawatts, considered as a fallback anchor. petroleumnews.com search returned 403 and stakenergy.com returned an empty page. No openable source states any capacity figure.
Alaska has eight data centers across five markets. Sole source is the same partisan outlet; datacentermap.com returned 429 twice.

John Sims saying Enstar is evaluating whether it is prudent to add new customers, citing JBER housing and data center interest. Neither supplied source contains prudent, JBER or data center in connection with Sims. The strongest residue is C24.
AEA as the source for the 4.6 mile tunnel. The number survives at C15 under Petroleum News; the AEA attribution dies.
AEA as the source for the 30,000 homes, 1.5 Bcf and five utilities figures. Only the 10 percent Railbelt share is confirmed on AEA's own page at C13.
Any absolute post-project generation figure. No document states one. The only honest path is the labelled arithmetic at C26.
warnings: THE HONESTY FIREWALL. Nothing in any fetched document links the Dixon Diversion to data centers. AEA's pages, the FERC notice and Petroleum News make zero mention of data centers or AI. The Air Force material and the Bradley Lake material are entirely separate records with no shared actor, document or docket. The danger is adjacency. If a slide places C08 or C26 immediately beside C20 with no separating language, a reader will infer the glacier is being diverted to power data centers. The deck REQUIRES an explicit slide stating that AEA has not said the project is for data centers and that these are two independent facts about magnitude.

TWO DIFFERENT $400 MILLION FIGURES, thirty five years apart, that happen to match. C09 is the new project. AEA's Bradley Lake page lists the original 1991 budget at $400 Million. Any slide showing $400 million must say which one it means.

CAPACITY VERSUS ENERGY IS THE DECK'S MOST LIKELY FACTUAL ERROR. 0.3 MW is a capacity gain of about a quarter of one percent. 38 percent is an energy gain. Both are true and not in conflict, because the diversion adds water rather than turbines. C07 must never appear without C08 on the same slide.

ACRES ARE NOT MEGAWATTS. With the 100 MW minimum dropped, there is no verified power figure attached to the Air Force offer at all. Any slide implying the Air Force offer represents a specific electrical load is unsupported. The honest comparison is between physical and financial effort, not between two megawatt numbers.

EVERY FORWARD-LOOKING NUMBER IS THE APPLICANT'S. The 38 percent, the $400 million, the six year schedule, the 30,000 homes and the 1.5 Bcf are projections by the sponsor or its trade-press summary, none independently reviewed. FERC accepting an application for filing is a procedural step and NOT an approval. Do not write that FERC approved anything.
C24 MUST NOT APPEAR IN QUOTATION MARKS. Setting the reporter's paraphrase as a Sims pull quote would be a fabricated quotation. Use C25 if the deck wants a Sims quote.
C26 IS OUR ARITHMETIC and must be labelled as such on the slide and in the caption.

SOURCES THAT WOULD NOT OPEN, disclosed rather than guessed around. SAM.gov, petroleumnews.com search, datacentermap.com, stakenergy.com, the EIA electricity data browser, and FERC eLibrary for P-8221. No figure here is sourced to the Final Amendment Application itself.
